From Sand to Window: A Short History of Glass

A  Glass is so ordinary today that it is easy to forget how remarkable it is. It is made largely from sand, one of the most common materials on Earth, and yet for most of human history it was a luxury. The basic ingredients have changed surprisingly little over four thousand years: silica, usually in the form of sand; a flux such as soda or potash, which lowers the temperature at which the silica melts; and lime, which makes the finished material stable and stops it from slowly dissolving in water. What has changed enormously is the skill and the technology used to turn these ingredients into useful objects.

B  The earliest objects made entirely of glass appear to be small beads produced in Mesopotamia in the third millennium BCE. Archaeologists think that glass may first have been discovered as a by-product of other high-temperature crafts, such as metalworking or the production of glazed pottery, in which a glassy coating forms on the surface of clay. By around 1500 BCE, craftspeople in Mesopotamia and Egypt were making small vessels by a technique known as core-forming. A core of clay and dung was shaped on the end of a metal rod and dipped in, or wrapped with, molten glass. When the glass had cooled, the core was scraped out, leaving a hollow container. These vessels were small, colourful and opaque, and they were mainly used to hold perfumes and oils for wealthy households.

C  The real revolution came in the first century BCE, somewhere on the eastern coast of the Mediterranean, when someone discovered that a gather of molten glass on the end of a hollow tube could be inflated with the breath. Glassblowing was dramatically faster than any earlier method, and it allowed thin, transparent vessels to be produced in large numbers. Within a few generations the technique had spread across the Roman Empire. Glass cups, bottles and storage jars became common in ordinary Roman homes, and some Roman buildings even had small panes of cast glass set into their windows, although these were thick and far from perfectly clear.

D  After the decline of the western Roman Empire, glass production continued, but the most celebrated centre of the craft eventually became Venice. In 1291 the city authorities ordered the glass furnaces to be moved to the nearby island of Murano. The official reason was the danger of fire in a crowded city built largely of wood, but the move also made it easier to protect the secrets of the trade. Skilled glassmakers enjoyed high social status, yet they were for long periods forbidden to leave the Venetian Republic. In the fifteenth century, Murano workshops developed a very clear, nearly colourless glass known as cristallo, which was achieved by carefully purifying the plant ash that served as the flux.

E  Other regions developed their own specialities. In England in the 1670s, George Ravenscroft obtained a patent for a glass containing lead oxide. This 'lead crystal' was heavier and softer than Venetian glass, which made it ideal for cutting, and it scattered light in a way that made it sparkle. Meanwhile, the growing demand for window glass led to new ways of producing flat sheets. In the crown method, a bubble of glass was spun until it opened out into a large disc; in the cylinder method, a long tube of blown glass was cut open and flattened. Both techniques left the glass slightly uneven, which is why many old windows distort the view behind them.

F  The problem of producing perfectly flat glass cheaply was not fully solved until the 1950s, when the float process was developed in Britain. In this method, molten glass is poured continuously onto a bath of molten tin. Because the glass floats on the smooth metal surface, it spreads out into a sheet with two perfectly parallel faces, and it requires no grinding or polishing. Float glass now accounts for the vast majority of the flat glass produced worldwide and is used in everything from office towers to car windscreens and mobile phone screens.

G  The history of glass is therefore not simply a story of beautiful objects. It is also a story of how small technical breakthroughs, often made by anonymous workers, gradually transformed a rare luxury into one of the most widely used materials of the modern world.

A  By the time they start school, most children have mastered the basic sound system of their language, know several thousand words and can produce complex sentences that they have never heard before. B  The process begins earlier than many parents realise. Research using techniques that measure where infants look, or how vigorously they suck on a dummy, has shown that newborn babies already prefer the sound of their mother's voice and of their native language over a foreign one. This suggests that some learning takes place before birth, since the rhythm and melody of speech can be heard, in muffled form, inside the womb. In the first months of life, infants can distinguish between speech sounds used in all the world's languages. By around their first birthday, however, they become less sensitive to contrasts that do not matter in the language around them. A baby growing up hearing Japanese, for example, gradually loses the ability to hear the difference between the English sounds 'r' and 'l'.

C  One of the puzzles of early learning is how infants discover where one word ends and the next begins, because in natural speech there are rarely pauses between words. A famous series of experiments in the 1990s suggested that babies keep track of statistical patterns. Eight-month-old infants listened to a continuous stream of invented syllables for just two minutes. Within that stream, certain syllables always followed one another, while others were combined only occasionally. Afterwards, the infants listened longer to sequences that crossed these boundaries, indicating that they had noticed which syllables belonged together. This ability to detect patterns is not, of course, the whole story, but it shows that infants are far more active learners than was once assumed.

D  Vocabulary growth is slow at first. Many children produce their first recognisable word at around twelve months and may know only fifty words six months later. After this point, however, many children experience what is often called a 'vocabulary spurt', adding several new words every day. At the same time, they begin to combine words into short phrases such as 'more juice' or 'daddy gone'. Interestingly, children's errors reveal a great deal about what they are learning. A child who says 'I goed' or 'two mouses' has clearly not copied these forms from adults; instead, the child has worked out a general rule and is applying it too widely.

E  Such evidence has fuelled a long debate. Some linguists argue that humans are born with specialised mental structures for language, which would explain how children acquire complex grammar from limited and often untidy input. Others maintain that general learning abilities, combined with the rich social environment in which children grow up, are sufficient. Most researchers today accept that both biology and experience play a role, although they continue to disagree about the balance between them.

F  What is less controversial is that the quantity and quality of language children hear matters.
